hypothesis: establish the reference point the session is measured against
observation: rmse=0.013345 against a target sd of 0.014184, i.e. R^2 ~= 0.115; trip_rmse=0.003037 against a trip-total sd of 0.0955. Trained in 7.1s of a 600s budget.
reasoning: The scaffold explains barely a tenth of link-rate variance and uses 1.2% of the time budget, so both capacity and features are wide open. Link rate is dominated by dynamics the three instantaneous features cannot express.

description: swap RandomForest for HistGradientBoosting, 300 iters, same 3 features
hypothesis: a 20-tree depth-10 forest is under-capacity; 300 boosting rounds should fit the speed/grade/miles surface much more finely and cut rmse
observation: a dead tie: rmse 0.013345 -> 0.013343 (-0.01%) and trip_rmse 0.003037 -> 0.003038 (+0.03%), both inside the +/-0.25% tie band, in 8.0s vs 7.1s
reasoning: Two very different learners land on the same number, so both have already saturated the information in these three features — the ceiling is the feature set, not model capacity. Model-family experiments are worthless until the features carry more signal; revert and spend the budget on features first.

description: add dke_per_mile = (v_next^2 - v_prev^2)/miles from neighbour link speeds
hypothesis: the energy balance has an acceleration term the instantaneous (speed, grade, length) triple cannot express; the neighbouring links' speeds bracket the link and give the kinetic-energy change across it directly
reasoning: Link-rate variance is dominated by vehicle dynamics, not by steady-state speed/grade. One physics-derived context feature more than halves the error, which reframes the whole session: the payoff is in sequence context, not in the learner.

description: add v_in (entry speed from the previous link)
hypothesis: regen recovers only part of braking energy while acceleration costs more than the kinetic energy it buys, so the same dke_per_mile is worth different energy at different entry speeds; the signed difference alone cannot say which
observation: rmse -1.71% (0.007317 -> 0.007192) but trip_rmse +0.26% (0.002329 -> 0.002335), which lands a hair outside the 0.25% tolerance the decision rule allows for the secondary metric
reasoning: The feature is real -- 1.7% is far outside noise on the primary metric -- but the 20-tree depth-10 forest has to spend splits on it and apparently loses a little of the mileage-weighted accuracy trip_rmse cares about. Discarded on the rule as written; flagged to re-test once model capacity is raised, since a depth-10 forest with 5 informative features is now the likely bottleneck.

description: swap RandomForest for HistGradientBoosting (identical config to exp1, now with dke_per_mile present)
hypothesis: exp1 found the learner irrelevant when the features carried almost no signal; with a strong dynamics feature there is now a real function to fit, so the extra capacity should finally pay
observation: rmse -2.54% (0.007317 -> 0.007131) and trip_rmse -5.32% (0.002329 -> 0.002205), from the exact model change that was a dead tie in exp1
reasoning: Capacity only matters once the features carry signal -- the same swap was worth 0.0% at 3 features and 2.5%/5.3% at 4. Model-family and hyperparameter experiments should therefore always be re-run after a big feature win, and the reverse ordering wastes runs.

hypothesis: exp4 showed capacity pays once features carry signal, so 8x wider trees should keep paying
observation: the two metrics split: rmse +0.45% (worse) while trip_rmse -0.63% (better), at double the runtime (8.9s -> 17.0s)
reasoning: Deeper trees start fitting the per-link noise -- the link rate of a 0.02-mile link is a ratio with a tiny denominator and is genuinely noisy -- which costs link rmse, while the extra resolution still helps the mileage-weighted trip total where the noise averages out. Capacity is already near its sweet spot at 4 features; the two metrics will keep disagreeing about it, and rmse is primary.

description: add dke_in_link, the entry-half of the kinetic-energy change ((v^2 - v_in^2)/miles)
hypothesis: accelerating and regenerating are not the same price, so a link that speeds up then slows down burns energy even at zero net dKE; the total alone cannot express that, but total plus one half locates the change inside the link
reasoning: Confirms the asymmetry hypothesis: it is not the net kinetic-energy change that costs energy but its decomposition into an accelerate leg and a brake leg. Suggests the remaining dynamics signal is about *shape within the link*, so finer sequence context (a stop before the link, the neighbour-of-neighbour) is the next place to look.

description: add gap_seconds, the idle time between the previous link ending and this one starting
hypothesis: a non-zero gap means the vehicle actually stopped, so the true entry speed was 0 and the entry kinetic energy had to be rebuilt -- the previous link's average speed cannot reveal that
observation: rmse -4.76% (0.006653 -> 0.006336) and trip_rmse -2.24% (0.002147 -> 0.002099); the probe had predicted only -3.6% for this feature in isolation
reasoning: It beat its isolated estimate because it corrects the entry speed that dke_in_link is built from -- the two interact. Every feature that resolves *what actually happened between links* keeps paying, which points at a sequence model as the general form of this whole family.

description: add prev_miles, the length of the previous link
hypothesis: the previous link's length sets how much road the entry speed change was spread over; the same entry speed reached over a mile and over fifty feet are different accelerations
observation: rmse -7.88% (0.006336 -> 0.005837) and trip_rmse -1.62% (0.002099 -> 0.002065), more than double the -3.6% the isolated probe predicted
reasoning: Like gap_seconds, it beat its isolated estimate because it conditions a feature already present rather than adding independent signal -- it tells the model how much to trust dke_in_link's implicit 'the change happened on this link' assumption. Cumulative rmse is now -56% from baseline, entirely from link-sequence context.

description: add next_miles, the length of the next link
hypothesis: the exit-side mirror of prev_miles: the next link's length sets how much road the exit speed change is spread over
observation: rmse -1.52% (0.005837 -> 0.005748) but trip_rmse essentially flat at -0.05%, five times weaker than the entry-side mirror image
reasoning: The entry side matters much more than the exit side, which fits the physics: energy spent accelerating into a link is paid on that link, while braking out of it is partly recovered by regen and partly charged to the next link. Asymmetry between entry and exit is a real property of this target, not an artefact.
